title: Apply knowledge of refrigeration and cold chain management for perishable produce exportation

lessons.title: Why the cold chain exists and the law behind it
lessons.html:
Background and necessity of the cold chain

South Africa exports citrus, grapes, apples, pears, stone fruit, avocados and other fresh produce to markets in Europe, the UK, the Middle East, Asia and North America. Many of these are two to five weeks away by ship. Fruit is alive after harvest. It keeps breathing, losing water and ageing. Without cooling, a carton of plums or grapes would be soft, shrivelled or rotten long before it reached a supermarket shelf overseas.

The cold chain is the unbroken series of cooled steps from the orchard to the retailer: cooling in the packhouse, cold storage, refrigerated truck, port cold store, reefer container or reefer ship, and the importer's cold store. Every link must hold the right temperature. If one link breaks, for example a pallet left on a hot loading bay for three hours, the damage cannot be reversed later.

Legislation that regulates the cold chain

Two main laws govern perishable exports:

  • The Perishable Products Export Control Act 9 of 1983 established the Perishable Products Export Control Board (PPECB). Its objectives include ensuring the orderly export of perishable products and controlling the handling, cooling and transport of these products so that they arrive in good condition. PPECB sets and monitors cold chain requirements for cold stores, containers and vessels and issues the related certificates.
  • The Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 sets quality, packing and marking standards for regulated agricultural products sold for export. PPECB carries out export inspections under this Act as an assignee of the national Department of Agriculture.

Phytosanitary rules, set by the importing country and administered through the national Department of Agriculture, also affect the cold chain. Some markets require a cold treatment, where fruit is held below a set temperature for a set number of days to kill fruit fly or false codling moth larvae. The exact protocol depends on the market and product and must be followed exactly.

The purpose of all this legislation is simple: protect consumers, protect the reputation of South African fruit and keep markets open for every grower.

lessons.title: Physiology of fruit and the storage environment
lessons.html:
Basic physiological processes

Harvested produce is still a living organism. Four processes decide how long it lasts:

  • Respiration: the fruit burns its own sugars and acids using oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide, water and heat. The faster it respires, the faster it ages.
  • Transpiration: water evaporates through the skin. Loss of water causes shrivelling, soft fruit, brown stems on grapes and weight loss, which is lost money.
  • Ethylene production and ripening: ethylene is a natural ripening gas. Climacteric fruit such as apples, pears, avocados, mangoes and stone fruit have a burst of respiration and ethylene as they ripen. Non-climacteric fruit such as citrus, grapes and litchis do not ripen further after harvest; they only age.
  • Senescence: the final ageing and breakdown of tissue, ending in decay.

How storage conditions affect these processes

FactorEffect
TemperatureLower temperature slows respiration, ripening and rot. As a rule, rate of deterioration rises quickly as temperature rises.
Relative humidityHigh humidity reduces water loss. Too wet can encourage mould.
AtmosphereLower oxygen and higher carbon dioxide (controlled atmosphere) slow respiration further.
EthyleneEthylene in the store speeds ripening and yellowing; ventilation or scrubbing removes it.

Too cold is also a problem

Every product has a lowest safe temperature. Below it, sensitive fruit suffers chilling injury: for example woolly texture in peaches and nectarines, skin browning in avocados and mangoes, and rind pitting in some citrus. Freezing damage happens below the fruit's freezing point. The correct set point is the one in the approved protocol for that product, variety and market, not simply the coldest the store can go.

A supervisor's job is to make sure fruit is cooled quickly after harvest, kept at its correct temperature and humidity, and not mixed with produce that gives off a lot of ethylene if it is sensitive to it.

lessons.title: Refrigeration principles, measurement and cold chain equipment
lessons.html:
How refrigeration works

Refrigeration does not add cold; it removes heat. A refrigerant circulates through four main parts:

  1. Evaporator inside the cold room: liquid refrigerant evaporates and absorbs heat from the air blown over the coils.
  2. Compressor: compresses the refrigerant gas, raising its pressure and temperature.
  3. Condenser outside: the hot gas gives off its heat to the outside air or water and turns back to liquid.
  4. Expansion valve: drops the pressure so the liquid can evaporate again in the evaporator.

Large South African packhouses often use ammonia systems; containers and smaller rooms use other refrigerants. Fans move cold air through the stacks, so correct stacking with air gaps matters as much as the machine.

Cooling methods

  • Room cooling: slow; suited to holding product already cold.
  • Forced-air cooling (precooling): fans pull cold air through vented cartons on pallets; much faster.
  • Hydrocooling: cold water, used for some stone fruit and vegetables.

Temperature measurement and controls

  • Pulp temperature is measured with a calibrated probe thermometer inserted into the fruit flesh. It tells you the real fruit temperature.
  • Air temperature: delivery air (leaving the evaporator) and return air (coming back from the product).
  • Data loggers travel with the fruit and record temperature for the whole journey.
  • Humidity sensors, and in CA stores oxygen and carbon dioxide analysers.
  • Thermometers and probes must be calibrated regularly, for example against an ice-water check, and records kept.

Cold chain infrastructure

  • Precoolers and cold rooms at the packhouse.
  • Refrigerated trucks and trailers.
  • Port cold stores and terminals.
  • Reefer containers with their own refrigeration unit, and conventional reefer vessels.
  • Loading docks with seals or curtains so warm air does not enter.

Maintenance equipment includes spare probes, calibration records, generator back-up, alarm systems and service records for compressors and fans.

Key points

  • The cold chain must be unbroken from packhouse to retailer.
  • The PPECB Act and the Agricultural Product Standards Act regulate export cold chain and quality.
  • Cold slows respiration, water loss and ripening, but too cold causes chilling injury.
  • Refrigeration removes heat via evaporator, compressor, condenser and expansion valve.
  • Pulp temperature from a calibrated probe is the true measure of fruit temperature.
